This adds the owner to the folder name and moves folder identity off the folder name entirely. - New import folders are named `{ownerName}-{spaceName}` under `import/`. - The owner name is resolved from space membership — `LocalAccess` for the source `space_id`, joined to `my_accounts` filtered on `agent_type = "person"`. Node authors are deliberately not used: they tell us who wrote a given node, which can differ from the account the source space belongs to. - The owner prefix is dropped when it adds nothing: Obsidian defaults the account name to the vault name, which is also the space name, so without this the folder would read `my-vault-my-vault` for anyone who has not set a username in settings. Same fallback when the owner lookup returns nothing, so a blocked query or a space with no person account degrades to the old `{spaceName}` naming rather than failing. - Folder identity comes from `.dg.metadata` (`spaceUri`, `spaceName`, optional `userName`) rather than the folder name, so a user who renames an import folder keeps it — the next import finds it again by `spaceUri` and reuses it instead of creating a duplicate. - Pre-existing folders with no `.dg.metadata` whose name matches the space name are adopted by writing metadata into them, rather than being abandoned. - Duplicate metadata pointing at the same `spaceUri` is resolved by keeping the more recently modified one. ## Out of scope Dropped or deferred after review discussion: - **Auto-migration of existing import folders** — removed (72bf26dc). name and does not say whose vault it was. This adds the owner to the folder name and moves folder identity off the folder name entirely. - New import folders are named `{ownerName}-{spaceName}` under `import/`. - The owner name is resolved from space membership — `LocalAccess` for the source `space_id`, joined to `my_accounts` filtered on `agent_type = "person"`. Node authors are deliberately not used: they tell us who wrote a given node, which can differ from the account the source space belongs to. - The owner prefix is dropped when it adds nothing: Obsidian defaults the account name to the vault name, which is also the space name, so without this the folder would read `my-vault-my-vault` for anyone who has not set a username in settings. Same fallback when the owner lookup returns nothing, so a blocked query or a space with no person account degrades to the old `{spaceName}` naming rather than failing. - Folder identity comes from `.dg.metadata` (`spaceUri`, `spaceName`, optional `userName`) rather than the folder name, so a user who renames an import folder keeps it — the next import finds it again by `spaceUri` and reuses it instead of creating a duplicate. - Pre-existing folders with no `.dg.metadata` whose name matches the space name are adopted by writing metadata into them, rather than being abandoned. - Duplicate metadata pointing at the same `spaceUri` is resolved by keeping the more recently modified one. ## Out of scope Dropped or deferred after review discussion: - **Auto-migration of existing import folders** — removed (72bf26dc). 1130 ENG-1656 Rename folder for imported vault CONFLICTING
https://www.loom.com/share/39deddfaa529440d96484590a8c0d53f

> Note: the Loom predates review feedback — it shows the original `{owner}-{spaceName}` naming plus the auto-migration that has since been dropped.

## Summary

Imported vaults all landed in `import/{spaceName}`, which is just the source vault's name and does not say whose vault it was. This adds the owner to the folder name and moves folder identity off the folder name entirely.

- New import folders are named `{ownerName}-{spaceName}` under `import/`.
- The owner name is resolved from space membership — `LocalAccess` for the source `space_id`, joined to `my_accounts` filtered on `agent_type = "person"`. Node authors are deliberately not used: they tell us who wrote a given node, which can differ from the account the source space belongs to.
- The owner prefix is dropped when it adds nothing: Obsidian defaults the account name to the vault name, which is also the space name, so without this the folder would read `my-vault-my-vault` for anyone who has not set a username in settings. Same fallback when the owner lookup returns nothing, so a blocked query or a space with no person account degrades to the old `{spaceName}` naming rather than failing.
- Folder identity comes from `.dg.metadata` (`spaceUri`, `spaceName`, optional `userName`) rather than the folder name, so a user who renames an import folder keeps it — the next import finds it again by `spaceUri` and reuses it instead of creating a duplicate.
- Pre-existing folders with no `.dg.metadata` whose name matches the space name are adopted by writing metadata into them, rather than being abandoned.
- Duplicate metadata pointing at the same `spaceUri` is resolved by keeping the more recently modified one.

## Out of scope

Dropped or deferred after review discussion:

- **Auto-migration of existing import folders** — removed (72bf26dc). Existing folders keep their names; only new imports use the new scheme. This also removes the `migrated` metadata flag that came up in review.
- **Username changes after import** — flagged by @maparent; the folder is not renamed when the owner's username changes. Separate, low priority.
- **Renaming or moving the `import` root** — `IMPORT_ROOT` is a fixed path and only its immediate children are scanned, so moving the root or nesting import folders deeper hides existing imports and the next import recreates them. Recorded as a known limitation in the code (0f388d81).
- **Multi-user (Roam) source vaults** — @maparent's point that owner-in-name suits mono-user vaults and a platform prefix may be the better shape for Roam. Not addressed here since only Obsidian vaults are shared today.

## Test plan

Automated (run on the merge result, current `main` merged in):

- [x] `tsc --noEmit` clean for `apps/obsidian`
- [x] `eslint` clean on both changed files (0 errors, 0 new warnings)

Manual — needs a re-check since the naming rules changed after the Loom was recorded:

- [ ] Import from a space whose owner has a username set in settings → `import/{username}-{spaceName}/`
- [ ] Import from a space whose owner has no username set (name defaults to vault name) → `import/{spaceName}/`, not `import/{spaceName}-{spaceName}/`
- [ ] Rename an import folder, then import from that space again → the renamed folder is reused, no duplicate created
- [ ] Existing `import/{spaceName}/` with no `.dg.metadata` → adopted, metadata written, folder not renamed

https://www.loom.com/share/39deddfaa529440d96484590a8c0d53f

> Note: the Loom predates review feedback — it shows the original `{owner}-{spaceName}` naming plus the auto-migration that has since been dropped.

## Summary

Imported vaults all landed in `import/{spaceName}`, which is just the source vault's name and does not say whose vault it was. This adds the owner to the folder name and moves folder identity off the folder name entirely.

- New import folders are named `{ownerName}-{spaceName}` under `import/`.
- The owner name is resolved from space membership — `LocalAccess` for the source `space_id`, joined to `my_accounts` filtered on `agent_type = "person"`. Node authors are deliberately not used: they tell us who wrote a given node, which can differ from the account the source space belongs to.
- The owner prefix is dropped when it adds nothing: Obsidian defaults the account name to the vault name, which is also the space name, so without this the folder would read `my-vault-my-vault` for anyone who has not set a username in settings. Same fallback when the owner lookup returns nothing, so a blocked query or a space with no person account degrades to the old `{spaceName}` naming rather than failing.
- Folder identity comes from `.dg.metadata` (`spaceUri`, `spaceName`, optional `userName`) rather than the folder name, so a user who renames an import folder keeps it — the next import finds it again by `spaceUri` and reuses it instead of creating a duplicate.
- Pre-existing folders with no `.dg.metadata` whose name matches the space name are adopted by writing metadata into them, rather than being abandoned.
- Duplicate metadata pointing at the same `spaceUri` is resolved by keeping the more recently modified one.

## Out of scope

Dropped or deferred after review discussion:

- **Auto-migration of existing import folders** — removed (72bf26dc). Existing folders keep their names; only new imports use the new scheme. This also removes the `migrated` metadata flag that came up in review.
- **Username changes after import** — flagged by @maparent; the folder is not renamed when the owner's username changes. Separate, low priority.
- **Renaming or moving the `import` root** — `IMPORT_ROOT` is a fixed path and only its immediate children are scanned, so moving the root or nesting import folders deeper hides existing imports and the next import recreates them. Recorded as a known limitation in the code (0f388d81).
- **Multi-user (Roam) source vaults** — @maparent's point that owner-in-name suits mono-user vaults and a platform prefix may be the better shape for Roam. Not addressed here since only Obsidian vaults are shared today.

## Test plan

Automated (run on the merge result, current `main` merged in):

- [x] `tsc --noEmit` clean for `apps/obsidian`
- [x] `eslint` clean on both changed files (0 errors, 0 new warnings)

Manual — needs a re-check since the naming rules changed after the Loom was recorded:

- [ ] Import from a space whose owner has a username set in settings → `import/{username}-{spaceName}/`
- [ ] Import from a space whose owner has no username set (name defaults to vault name) → `import/{spaceName}/`, not `import/{spaceName}-{spaceName}/`
- [ ] Rename an import folder, then import from that space again → the renamed folder is reused, no duplicate created
- [ ] Existing `import/{spaceName}/` with no `.dg.metadata` → adopted, metadata written, folder not renamed

  * The way it was implemented did not allow to discern field absence

https://www.loom.com/share/39deddfaa529440d96484590a8c0d53f

> Note: the Loom predates review feedback — it shows the original `{owner}-{spaceName}` naming plus the auto-migration that has since been dropped.

## Summary

Imported vaults all landed in `import/{spaceName}`, which is just the source vault's name and does not say whose vault it was. This adds the owner to the folder name and moves folder identity off the folder name entirely.

- New import folders are named `{ownerName}-{spaceName}` under `import/`.
- The owner name is resolved from space membership — `LocalAccess` for the source `space_id`, joined to `my_accounts` filtered on `agent_type = "person"`. Node authors are deliberately not used: they tell us who wrote a given node, which can differ from the account the source space belongs to.
- The owner prefix is dropped when it adds nothing: Obsidian defaults the account name to the vault name, which is also the space name, so without this the folder would read `my-vault-my-vault` for anyone who has not set a username in settings. Same fallback when the owner lookup returns nothing, so a blocked query or a space with no person account degrades to the old `{spaceName}` naming rather than failing.
- Folder identity comes from `.dg.metadata` (`spaceUri`, `spaceName`, optional `userName`) rather than the folder name, so a user who renames an import folder keeps it — the next import finds it again by `spaceUri` and reuses it instead of creating a duplicate.
- Pre-existing folders with no `.dg.metadata` whose name matches the space name are adopted by writing metadata into them, rather than being abandoned.
- Duplicate metadata pointing at the same `spaceUri` is resolved by keeping the more recently modified one.

## Out of scope

Dropped or deferred after review discussion:

- **Auto-migration of existing import folders** — removed (72bf26dc). Existing folders keep their names; only new imports use the new scheme. This also removes the `migrated` metadata flag that came up in review.
- **Username changes after import** — flagged by @maparent; the folder is not renamed when the owner's username changes. Separate, low priority.
- **Renaming or moving the `import` root** — `IMPORT_ROOT` is a fixed path and only its immediate children are scanned, so moving the root or nesting import folders deeper hides existing imports and the next import recreates them. Recorded as a known limitation in the code (0f388d81).
- **Multi-user (Roam) source vaults** — @maparent's point that owner-in-name suits mono-user vaults and a platform prefix may be the better shape for Roam. Not addressed here since only Obsidian vaults are shared today.

## Test plan

Automated (run on the merge result, current `main` merged in):

- [x] `tsc --noEmit` clean for `apps/obsidian`
- [x] `eslint` clean on both changed files (0 errors, 0 new warnings)

Manual — needs a re-check since the naming rules changed after the Loom was recorded:

- [ ] Import from a space whose owner has a username set in settings → `import/{username}-{spaceName}/`
- [ ] Import from a space whose owner has no username set (name defaults to vault name) → `import/{spaceName}/`, not `import/{spaceName}-{spaceName}/`
- [ ] Rename an import folder, then import from that space again → the renamed folder is reused, no duplicate created
- [ ] Existing `import/{spaceName}/` with no `.dg.metadata` → adopted, metadata written, folder not renamed

I’m expanding the matrix along three dimensions: all four directions (R→R, R→O, O→R, O→O), different users and group memberships, and changes after the first import.

The most valuable combined-work case is three-space collaboration: A shares a node, B imports it and relates a new B-owned node to it, then A and C import B’s node. That checks origin identity, access to both endpoints, schema acceptance, and relation deduplication together. I’ll also include two users editing the same Roam source graph, since that exercises sync ownership and authorship in a way separate-vault tests don’t.

**The ticket names the wrong attribute.** Asset re-upload is gated by `getSharedRoamNodesWithFullContentUpdatesSince`, which matches a node when either the page's own `:edit/time` or its `:page/edit-time` is newer than the watermark. `:page/edit-time` tracks the latest edit anywhere on the page, descendant blocks included. The ticket says the page's own `:edit/time` is what the query reads. That is true of the node-row query, not of the content path the assets travel on.

**A bump without props works, but the obvious version is unsafe.** Measured:

| write | moves `:page/edit-time` | moves page `:edit/time` | touches `:edit/user` |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| rewrite a block with its own string | yes | no | **yes** |
| `props` on a block | yes | no | no |
| `props` on the page | yes | yes | no |
| create then delete a scratch child block | yes | no | no |
| rewrite the page with its own title | no | no | no |
| set `:page/edit-time` or `:edit/time` directly, four spellings | no | no | no |

Rewriting a block with its own string is the cheapest bump and it does move the time. It also reassigns `:edit/user`, and the replacement has no `:user/display-name`, so the sync would publish that node's `author_name` as "Anonymous User". That was confirmed against a real block, not a fixture. It is not an option.

That leaves two: create and delete a scratch child block, or a `props` write.

**The question.** Your wording may rule out `props` entirely. The intent read more as reducing complexity, and on that measure `props` is the simpler of the two options left.

A `props` write on the node's first child is one atomic write. It moves only `:page/edit-time`, so only the content path re-runs and the node row is left alone. It leaves `:edit/user` untouched, verified on September 18 against a block another user last edited. Writing the same constant value twice still moves the time, so the value is a constant, nothing ever reads it back, and there is no attempt count, no limit, and no per-node state.

Create-and-delete a scratch child block is the alternative. That is two writes with a state in between, and if the sync dies there it leaves an empty bullet behind on the user's page, which is the visible residue this approach is meant to avoid. More moving parts, not fewer.

| write | moves `:page/edit-time` | moves page `:edit/time` | touches `:edit/user` |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| rewrite a block with its own string | yes | no | **yes** |
| `props` on a block | yes | no | no |
| `props` on the page | yes | yes | no |
| create then delete a scratch child block | yes | no | no |
| rewrite the page with its own title | no | no | no |
| set `:page/edit-time` or `:edit/time` directly, four spellings | no | no | no |

**The ticket names the wrong attribute.** Asset re-upload is gated by `getSharedRoamNodesWithFullContentUpdatesSince`, which matches a node when either the page's own `:edit/time` or its `:page/edit-time` is newer than the watermark. `:page/edit-time` tracks the latest edit anywhere on the page, descendant blocks included. **A bump without props works, but the obvious version is unsafe.** Measured:

| write | moves `:page/edit-time` | moves page `:edit/time` | touches `:edit/user` |
| -- | -- | -- | -- |
| rewrite a block with its own string | yes | no | **yes** |
| `props` on a block | yes | no | no |
| `props` on the page | yes | yes | no |
| create then delete a scratch child block | yes | no | no |
| rewrite the page with its own title | no | no | no |
| set `:page/edit-time` or `:edit/time` directly, four spellings | no | no | no |

Rewriting a block with its own string is the cheapest bump and it does move the time. It also reassigns `:edit/user`, and the replacement has no `:user/display-name`, so the sync would publish that node's `author_name` as "Anonymous User". name: scope-check
description: Compare a pull request or Git diff with a Linear engineering ticket's Done When criteria and produce a copy-ready PR scope check. Use when preparing or reviewing a PR, checking whether an implementation introduced broader abstractions or unsupported cases, or documenting why added scope is required now.
---

# Scope Check

Compare the completed change with its acceptance boundary. Return a copy-ready `Scope check` section unless the user requests the analysis too.

## Gather the Inputs

1. Resolve the Linear issue from an explicit `ENG-###` identifier, then from the PR or branch name. Fetch the issue with the Linear connector. If it is unavailable, ask for the ticket's `Problem`, `Solution`, and `Done When` sections.
2. Treat `Done When` as the acceptance boundary. Use `Problem` and `Solution` only to clarify that boundary, not to silently expand it.
3. Resolve the final change set from the supplied diff or PR. For a PR, inspect its metadata and complete diff. For the current branch, compare it with the PR base branch and include staged and unstaged changes.
4. Read linked decisions or ticket comments only when they explain an apparent scope expansion.

## Evaluate Scope

Map every material behavior or architectural change to a `Done When` criterion.

- Treat implementation details, tests, documentation, and generated files required to satisfy `Done When` as in scope.
- Flag broader abstractions, unrelated refactors, new dependencies, migrations, or support for cases not required by `Done When`.
- Do not treat a change as in scope only because it is useful or adjacent.

For each scope expansion, determine:

1. What broader abstraction or additional case was introduced?
2. Which current use case or ticket requires it, and why must it be included now rather than deferred?
3. Was anyone affected or consulted, and where is the discussion or decision recorded?

Do not invent missing justification. Mark it `Not documented` and recommend recording it in a Linear comment before the PR is merged.

## Format the Result

Use this form when the diff stays within scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: None.
```

Use this form when the diff expands scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: <what changed>
- Required now: <use case or ticket and why it cannot be deferred>
- Anyone affected or consulted: <Yes, No, or Not documented>
- Decision: <link to the discussion or decision, or `Not documented`>
```

If the ticket or diff cannot be resolved, leave the checkbox unchecked and state exactly what input is missing. Keep findings short and evidence-based.

Do not modify the issue, PR, or implementation unless the user explicitly asks.
## Reviewer brief

<!-- Optional. Remove this section when it adds no value.
Include only the fields that help the reviewer:
- Result: The final behavior or outcome.
- Review focus: A decision, risk, or part of the diff that needs careful review.
- Risk or follow-up: Unresolved, unverified, or deferred work that affects approval.
-->

## Verification

<!-- Optional checks and their results. Remove this section when it adds no value. -->

## Loom video

<!-- Include a short Loom video for every PR (any change—UI, backend, refactors, infra, etc.).
This helps reviewers understand intent quickly and catches issues earlier
- Keep it under 2–3 minutes
- Show before/after for bug fixes
- Narrate key design or dev decisions
- Paste the Loom link in the PR body
-->

## Scope check

- [ ] Ran `$scope-check` against the ENG ticket and final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`:

<!-- Add either:
- `None` when the final diff stays within Done When.
- What changed, why it is required now, whether anyone was affected or consulted, and links to the use case, ticket, or decision.
-->

## Standards check

- [ ] Ran `$dg-pr-adherence-check` against the final diff and PR metadata.

<!-- Checking the box means the review ran, not that every requirement passed.
Make any outstanding findings or unverified requirements known to the PR author
so they can address them. -->

## Local delegated full review

- [ ] Ran a comprehensive review of the entire final diff in a subagent with a fresh context. Use `$dg-delegated-full-review` when no other full-review workflow is available.

name: scope-check
description: Compare a pull request or Git diff with a Linear engineering ticket's Done When criteria and produce a copy-ready PR scope check. Use when preparing or reviewing a PR, checking whether an implementation introduced broader abstractions or unsupported cases, or documenting why added scope is required now.
---

# Scope Check

Compare the completed change with its acceptance boundary. Return a copy-ready `Scope check` section unless the user requests the analysis too.

## Gather the Inputs

1. Resolve the Linear issue from an explicit `ENG-###` identifier, then from the PR or branch name. Fetch the issue with the Linear connector. If it is unavailable, ask for the ticket's `Problem`, `Solution`, and `Done When` sections.
2. Treat `Done When` as the acceptance boundary. Use `Problem` and `Solution` only to clarify that boundary, not to silently expand it.
3. Resolve the final change set from the supplied diff or PR. For a PR, inspect its metadata and complete diff. For the current branch, compare it with the PR base branch and include staged and unstaged changes.
4. Read linked decisions or ticket comments only when they explain an apparent scope expansion.

## Evaluate Scope

Map every material behavior or architectural change to a `Done When` criterion.

- Treat implementation details, tests, documentation, and generated files required to satisfy `Done When` as in scope.
- Flag broader abstractions, unrelated refactors, new dependencies, migrations, or support for cases not required by `Done When`.
- Do not treat a change as in scope only because it is useful or adjacent.

For each scope expansion, determine:

1. What broader abstraction or additional case was introduced?
2. Which current use case or ticket requires it, and why must it be included now rather than deferred?
3. Was anyone affected or consulted, and where is the discussion or decision recorded?

Do not invent missing justification. Mark it `Not documented` and recommend recording it in a Linear comment before the PR is merged.

## Format the Result

Use this form when the diff stays within scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: None.
```

Use this form when the diff expands scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: <what changed>
- Required now: <use case or ticket and why it cannot be deferred>
- Anyone affected or consulted: <Yes, No, or Not documented>
- Decision: <link to the discussion or decision, or `Not documented`>
```

If the ticket or diff cannot be resolved, leave the checkbox unchecked and state exactly what input is missing. Keep findings short and evidence-based.

Do not modify the issue, PR, or implementation unless the user explicitly asks.
## Reviewer brief

<!-- Optional. Remove this section when it adds no value.
Include only the fields that help the reviewer:
- Result: The final behavior or outcome.
- Review focus: A decision, risk, or part of the diff that needs careful review.
- Risk or follow-up: Unresolved, unverified, or deferred work that affects approval.
-->

## Verification

<!-- Optional checks and their results. Remove this section when it adds no value. -->

## Loom video

<!-- Include a short Loom video for every PR (any change—UI, backend, refactors, infra, etc.).
This helps reviewers understand intent quickly and catches issues earlier
- Keep it under 2–3 minutes
- Show before/after for bug fixes
- Narrate key design or dev decisions
- Paste the Loom link in the PR body
-->

## Scope check

- [ ] Ran `$scope-check` against the ENG ticket and final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`:

<!-- Add either:
- `None` when the final diff stays within Done When.
- What changed, why it is required now, whether anyone was affected or consulted, and links to the use case, ticket, or decision.
-->

so they can address them. -->

+
+**What the project promises**
+
+The [current Linear project](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/project/push-and-pull-nodes-between-roam-and-obsidian-49473d9eeb09) defines a group-targeted, single-node publish flow through shared persistence. Existing source sync keeps already-shared content fresh. Destination discovery, import, and refresh are explicit. A refresh may overwrite edits to the imported copy. Multiple selected imports are supported.

+Required dependencies include the node's schema, resolvable assets, Source where accessible, and eligible relations whose endpoints can resolve. +| Route | Source | Destination |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| RR | Roam graph A | Roam graph B |
+| RO | Roam graph A | Obsidian vault B |
+| OR | Obsidian vault A | Roam graph B |
+| OO | Obsidian vault A | Obsidian vault B |

+Treat RO and OR as separate implementations. A successful round trip through converters is also different from a user completing publish, discovery, import, and refresh in the products.
+
+**People, spaces, and access**
+
+Use dedicated fixtures with known authors and a unique prefix such as `BB-20260925-<tester>-<case>`.
+
+| Actor | Role | Membership |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| A | Source author and fixture-group admin | G-team and G-other |
+| B | Collaborator/importer | G-team only |
+| C | Third collaborator | G-team and G-other |
+| X | Negative-access test account | Neither group |

A and B also need separate authenticated sessions in the same Roam source graph for C05/C06, and in the same Roam destination graph for C07. Product graph access and DG group membership must be recorded separately; sharing a Roam graph does not test isolation between DG groups.
+

+
+Use an isolated scratch vault for copied-vault identity tests. Multi-client Obsidian file synchronization is an additional host-product setup, not a DG promise.
+
+**Reusable fixture set**
+
+1. Source S with a citation, body text, and a known author.
+2. Evidence E referencing S; Evidence E2 also referencing S; a variant with no accessible Source.
+3. Claim C and Question Q; stored directed relations linking C, E, and Q.
+4. A custom node type with a format, Source role, and template body; one matching local type and one deliberately incompatible same-name type.
+5. Text payload with numbered version markers, nested blocks/lists, headings, paragraphs, code, links, tasks, and Unicode.
+6. Small valid PNG, PDF, audio, and video files. Reuse one file across nodes, and create different bytes with the same filename. Add valid boundary-size files around 6 MiB.

+8. A source node shared only to G-other and a public-to-G-team Evidence/relation that refers to it. This exercises dependency visibility without needing real private material.
+
+Record origin RIDs, local UIDs/paths, authors, groups, source timestamps, and content markers before each mutation. Shared storage inspection should use the same account permissions as the user action; an admin/service-role query cannot prove the recipient has correct access.
+
+**First-session order**
+
+Run workflows that reuse the same fixtures. The complete matrix is a coverage inventory, not a requirement to execute 346 separate setup procedures in one meeting.
+
+| Wave | Exercise | Cases covered | Route coverage |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| 1 | Publish a fresh text node, discover/import, repeat, edit upstream, manually refresh, rename | S01, I01, I08, U01, U02, U05 | All four directions |
+| 2 | Import Evidence alone with available, existing, and private/missing Source; repair a placeholder | D01–D04, S08 | All four directions; placeholder repair on RR/OR |
+| 3 | Add media after first share, refresh, reuse the asset, fail and retry one transfer | A01, A03, A07–A10, U10 | All four directions for media; route-specific retry paths |
+| 4 | Import a new relation schema and instance, accept separately, use on canvas | T02, T07–T12, T16 | All four directions, with both products' acceptance UIs |
+| 5 | A owns a; B imports a, relates owned b to a, publishes b; A and C import b | C01, C02, C11 | Start ROR and ORO; then homogeneous controls and remaining combinations |
+| 6 | Revoke access, test outsider reads, and recover after regrant | S04–S08, F01, F04 | Both destination products and both origin products |
+| 7 | Two users in one Roam graph: edit, asset retry, overlapping sync/import, provenance | C05–C08, A11 | Roam source to R/O; R/O source to shared Roam destination |
+| 8 | Target the known seams: IDs, normalized filenames, changed schema/Source, relation deletion | I07, I09, U11, T03, T14 | Each applicable path; resolve characterization questions |
+
+Check S10 before a Roam import session. With the current known command-gating gap, suggestive mode may need to be enabled to continue other cases. Record that prerequisite and leave S10 marked as the known gap; do not treat the workaround as a pass.
+
+Then use F05–F14 for the combined UX/recovery sweep and the remaining P1 cases for boundary coverage. Prioritize a distinct source/destination path over repeating an already covered actor/setup combination. Expand any failure across the other directions to establish its extent.
+
+**How to record a result**
+
+Record one result per case and route. Include candidate commit/build hashes, app versions, users and memberships, source/destination identifiers, fixture RIDs, before state, exact action, expected and actual behavior, and screenshot/log/storage evidence. A pass needs the visible result and stable identity/content; it cannot be inferred from a success toast alone.
+
+Use `Pass`, `Fail`, `Blocked`, `Decision needed`, or `Not run`. Record a known-gap failure against its existing issue. A blocked prerequisite is not a failed downstream feature. A characterization question needs a decision before an ambiguous outcome can be called a pass. Keep deferred polish separate from data loss, access leakage, wrong identity, unrecoverable partial imports, or broken core flows.
+
+A minimal useful bug report is: case + route + build; actors/groups; starting data; reproduction steps; expected versus actual; affected identity/content; evidence; workaround; existing related issue. Do not create duplicate tickets for behavior already covered by ENG-2297, ENG-2295, or the recorded asset retry limitations.
+
+After each destructive fixture operation, verify that only the named fixture changed. Preserve enough failed state to reproduce the problem, and record fixture cleanup separately from product behavior.
+
+**Proposed internal-release gate**
+
+Require core publish/import/refresh, Source, relation acceptance, media, access, and identity workflows in every applicable direction, plus the three-space and shared-Roam-user checks. Every open P0 failure needs a fix or an explicit team decision before calling the candidate ready. Product-policy questions and accepted limitations must be recorded rather than converted into assumed passes. This proposal does not mark the Linear validation task complete.
+
+Local type checks, unit tests, and compilation are prerequisites. This preparation does not yet prove runtime behavior, live RLS/storage access, schema deployment, or multi-user synchronization on the shared backend.

Record origin RIDs, local UIDs/paths, authors, groups, source timestamps, and content markers before each mutation. Shared storage inspection should use the same account permissions as the user action; an admin/service-role query cannot prove the recipient has correct access.

**First-session order**

Run workflows that reuse the same fixtures. The complete matrix is a coverage inventory, not a requirement to execute 346 separate setup procedures in one meeting.

| Wave | Exercise | Cases covered | Route coverage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Publish a fresh text node, discover/import, repeat, edit upstream, manually refresh, rename | S01, I01, I08, U01, U02, U05 | All four directions |
| 2 | Import Evidence alone with available, existing, and private/missing Source; repair a placeholder | D01–D04, S08 | All four directions; placeholder repair on RR/OR |
| 3 | Add media after first share, refresh, reuse the asset, fail and retry one transfer | A01, A03, A07–A10, U10 | All four directions for media; route-specific retry paths |
| 4 | Import a new relation schema and instance, accept separately, use on canvas | T02, T07–T12, T16 | All four directions, with both products' acceptance UIs |
| 5 | A owns a; B imports a, relates owned b to a, publishes b; A and C import b | C01, C02, C11 | Start ROR and ORO; then homogeneous controls and remaining combinations |
| 6 | Revoke access, test outsider reads, and recover after regrant | S04–S08, F01, F04 | Both destination products and both origin products |
| 7 | Two users in one Roam graph: edit, asset retry, overlapping sync/import, provenance | C05–C08, A11 | Roam source to R/O; R/O source to shared Roam destination |
| 8 | Target the known seams: IDs, normalized filenames, changed schema/Source, relation deletion | I07, I09, U11, T03, T14 | Each applicable path; resolve characterization questions |

Check S10 before a Roam import session. With the current known command-gating gap, suggestive mode may need to be enabled to continue other cases. Record that prerequisite and leave S10 marked as the known gap; do not treat the workaround as a pass.

Then use F05–F14 for the combined UX/recovery sweep and the remaining P1 cases for boundary coverage. Prioritize a distinct source/destination path over repeating an already covered actor/setup combination. Expand any failure across the other directions to establish its extent.

**How to record a result**

Record one result per case and route. Include candidate commit/build hashes, app versions, users and memberships, source/destination identifiers, fixture RIDs, before state, exact action, expected and actual behavior, and screenshot/log/storage evidence. A pass needs the visible result and stable identity/content; it cannot be inferred from a success toast alone.

Use `Pass`, `Fail`, `Blocked`, `Decision needed`, or `Not run`. Record a known-gap failure against its existing issue. A blocked prerequisite is not a failed downstream feature. A characterization question needs a decision before an ambiguous outcome can be called a pass. Keep deferred polish separate from data loss, access leakage, wrong identity, unrecoverable partial imports, or broken core flows.

A minimal useful bug report is: case + route + build; actors/groups; starting data; reproduction steps; expected versus actual; affected identity/content; evidence; workaround; existing related issue. Do not create duplicate tickets for behavior already covered by ENG-2297, ENG-2295, or the recorded asset retry limitations.

After each destructive fixture operation, verify that only the named fixture changed. Preserve enough failed state to reproduce the problem, and record fixture cleanup separately from product behavior.

Require core publish/import/refresh, Source, relation acceptance, media, access, and identity workflows in every applicable direction, plus the three-space and shared-Roam-user checks. Every open P0 failure needs a fix or an explicit team decision before calling the candidate ready. Product-policy questions and accepted limitations must be recorded rather than converted into assumed passes. This proposal does not mark the Linear validation task complete.

Local type checks, unit tests, and compilation are prerequisites. This preparation does not yet prove runtime behavior, live RLS/storage access, schema deployment, or multi-user synchronization on the shared backend.

I’ve assembled the combined candidate and written **100 test scenarios**, with steps, expected results, applicable directions, and links to the existing work.

The main artifacts are:

- **[Full test matrix](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925/validation/roam-obsidian-2026-09-25/TEST-MATRIX.md)** — all 100 scenarios.
- **[Setup and session order](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925/validation/roam-obsidian-2026-09-25/README.md)** — people, groups, fixtures, and a practical sequence.
- **[Baseline and known gaps](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925/validation/roam-obsidian-2026-09-25/BASELINE.md)** — exact PR heads, integration decisions, and unresolved expectations.

**The combined build is ready for internal testing. Manual product validation has not been run yet.**

The candidate is at commit `09d97321` on `validation/roam-obsidian-20260925`, in [this dedicated worktree](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925).

It combines current main with:

| PR | Included work |
|---|---|
| [#1383](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1383) | Review and accept imported relation types and triples |
| [#1475](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1475) | Consistent schema metadata between sync and publish |
| [#1477](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1477) | Retry failed Roam asset copies |
| [#1479](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1479) | Roam import dialog and feedback |
| [#1482](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1482) | Obsidian import filenames |
| [#1412](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1412) | Round-trip tests, adapted to current main |

The five runtime merges were clean. The older round-trip test stack needed small harness updates and the current `[[@placeholder]]` expectation. The explicitly iceboxed post-v0 refactors are excluded; the baseline records the other exclusions.

Loadable, production-configured bundles are available here:

- **[Roam extension folder](/home/sid/Downloads/roam-obsidian-bugbash-20260925-09d97321/roam)**
- **[Obsidian plugin folder](/home/sid/Downloads/roam-obsidian-bugbash-20260925-09d97321/obsidian)**

Frozen install, all eight workspace type-check tasks, all six unit-test tasks, and both builds pass. That includes **600 Roam tests and 87 Obsidian tests**. The exported bundles are hash-verified.

The testing model needs **four directed paths: RR, RO, OR, OO**. RO and OR exercise different implementations. Alongside those, we need multiple users in one Roam graph and three distinct collaborating spaces.

One expectation from Linear matters throughout: **source edits sync to shared storage; destination refresh is manual, and refresh may overwrite edits to the imported copy**. Automatic destination updates and bidirectional text merging are outside v0. This resolves the uncertainty about polling in the older sheet. [Project scope](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/project/push-and-pull-nodes-between-roam-and-obsidian-49473d9eeb09)

The inventory covers:

| Area | Cases | What we exercise |
|---|---:|---|
| Sharing and access | 12 | First publish, multiple groups, outsiders, revoked/restored access, private dependencies, login changes, sharing/suggestive-mode combinations |
| Import, content, and identity | 12 | Markdown structure, filenames, duplicate titles, repeated imports, mixed batches, equal local IDs from different spaces |
| Updates and refresh | 12 | Source edits, local edits, rename, refresh-all partial failures, deletion/recreation, asset changes, Source/schema-only changes |
| Assets | 12 | Images/PDF/audio/video, paths, deduplication, same filename with different bytes, replacement, size limits, failures and retries |
| Source documents | 10 | Automatic Source import, reuse, missing/private Sources, placeholder repair, multiple Sources, changed references, returning to an original Source |
| Schemas and relations | 16 | Existing/new types, metadata consistency, templates, provisional schemas, instance acceptance, missing endpoints, deletion, direction, canvas use |
| Collaboration | 12 | Three-space relations, private endpoints, cycles, fan-out, multiple Roam editors, overlapping sync/import, authorship, cloned identities |
| Recovery and combined UX | 14 | Partial batches, relations failing after nodes succeed, interruption/restart, sorting/selection, result links, provenance, returning to normal work |

Expanding every applicable direction gives **346 individual executions**. That is the coverage inventory; the session guide groups them into workflows that reuse fixtures.

The most valuable combined-work scenario is this:

1. **A publishes node `a`.**
2. **B imports `a`, creates its own node `b`, relates `b` to imported `a`, and publishes `b`.**
3. **A imports `b` and should connect it to its original `a`.**
4. **C imports both and should see the correct tentative relation between those origins.**

Then repeat with C lacking access to `a`, with renamed endpoints, and after acceptance and refresh. This simultaneously exercises origin identity, group access, endpoint mapping, schema acceptance, and deduplication. The matrix includes all eight three-space platform combinations.

A second essential workflow uses **two people in the same Roam source graph**: A publishes, B edits the body or adds an asset, and either client performs the sync. We need to verify freshness, retry behavior, and authorship together.

There are already several specific places to probe:

- **ENG-2297 remains unresolved.** The candidate still gates Roam import discovery on suggestive mode. This is a known gap to record separately from subsequent import tests.
- **Obsidian discovery may conflate equal local IDs from different spaces.** Discovery filters on the local ID alone, while materialization uses fuller identity. This is a source-based risk, not a live reproduction.
- **Node refresh does not establish relation reconciliation.** Upstream relation deletion, retargeting, and preservation of local acceptance need explicit testing and a clear expected policy.
- **Asset recovery differs by failure location.** Sync failures can retry automatically; publish failures require republishing; assets reached only through another page’s embed have an accepted retry limitation.
- **Source-only and schema-only changes need their own cases.** Timestamp-based skipping can make these behave differently from editing the Evidence body.

I’d start with the four basic publish/import/refresh paths, then Source and media regressions, relation acceptance, the three-space workflow, and the shared-Roam-user/access cases. Those combinations should expose the most consequential gaps between the separately completed features.

**Yes, a draft validation PR with one video per group of tests is a good fit here.** It gives us a concrete combined build, CI results, and one place for the team to inspect the work.

I’d add a small test-results table alongside the videos. The videos show what happened; the table makes coverage, failures, and remaining work easy to see.

The setup I’d use is:

1. **One draft integration PR for the combined candidate.** Its description names the included PRs and links to the test plan and loadable builds. We explicitly mark it as a validation branch, since its diff contains work already being reviewed in other PRs.
2. **Group tests around complete user workflows.** For example, publish → import → edit → refresh; Evidence with Sources and assets; or three-space collaboration with relations. Each recording follows a coherent workflow and identifies the cases it covers.
3. **One result entry per group and candidate version.** Record the commit, directions tested, pass/fail/blocked cases, video, and linked bugs.
4. **Fixes go into focused PRs.** We incorporate them into the combined candidate, rerun the affected group, and run a small cross-product smoke check.

The important detail is **pinning each recording to the build it tested**. Once we add another fix, an earlier video remains evidence for the earlier candidate. We should be able to tell which results still apply and which need a rerun.

For recording logistics, I’d capture the testing session as we execute it, then attach a short walkthrough of each completed group with timestamps or case IDs. That preserves useful failure evidence while giving reviewers something manageable to watch. A group with failures still gets a recording and an honest result.

There are three reasonable places to organize this:

| Approach | Strength | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| **Draft PR as the main home** | Code, build, CI, discussion, and videos are together | The combined diff can be noisy; the PR changes as its constituent PRs merge |
| **Linear validation ticket as the main home** | Stable place for progress, blockers, bugs, and the release decision | Needs links back to the exact candidate build |
| **Shared test sheet as the main home** | Easiest for several developers to record results simultaneously | Needs disciplined links to commits, evidence, and issues |

**My preference is a light hybrid: the draft PR holds the candidate and videos; the existing internal-validation ticket holds the overall outcome and blocking bugs.** We keep one authoritative results table and link to it from both.

For our first few videos, I’d group them like this:

- **Basic lifecycle:** all four directions, repeated import, upstream edits, refresh, and rename.
- **Sources and assets:** available/missing Source, placeholder repair, media, deduplication, and retry.
- **Relations and collaboration:** schema acceptance, instance acceptance, canvas use, and A → B → C.
- **Access and recovery:** private dependencies, revoked access, partial failure, and multiple users in one Roam graph.

That gives us a reviewable record of the combined product, with a clear route from a failed test to its fix and retest.

Results, videos, and one ticket per failure can live there, and they'll outlast the PRs. If you want one SHA everyone builds from, push the branch without opening a PR. pnpm ci:validate already passes on it locally.

2. Record user journeys, not test groups, and make each recording a test.
The video tooling can check results inside the recording, and it can show Roam and Obsidian side by side. So instead of about 15 groups × 4 directions, I'd do about 6 recordings:
- one per direction (RR, RO, OR, OO), each covering share → discover → import → edit at source → refresh → accept relation
- the three-space relation case from your sheet
- a round trip, Roam → Obsidian → Roam

Each recording then passes or fails on its checks, so you can re-run it after ENG-2131 or ENG-2296 changes. What it needs:
- It only runs against local Supabase.
- RR needs Playwright slot 2 logged back in, since the dev graph is read-only.
- Access tests need a second account that isn't in the group.
- Per your rule, recording happens in a separate session.

3. Videos show that something passed; they don't find gaps. Covering more cases does. I'd split the matrix three ways:
- Content conversion (markdown fidelity, title formatting both ways, source mapping, asset link rewrites, node identity): automated round-trip tests in CI across all four directions. It's the cheapest full coverage and keeps checking after merge. It extends ENG-2143, ENG-1879 and ENG-1880.
- Access and deletion (non-members can't see nodes, access removal, cleanup after a source is deleted): database tests on local Supabase. A video can't convincingly show that something is missing.
- UI, real data, several users in one graph: the team bug bash on real graphs. Record a short clip only when something fails, and attach it to that bug's ticket.

The code and ticket readers are still running. When they finish I'll build the matrix and tag each row with its lane (CI, recording, or manual), so you can choose which way to go.


ME::: maybe the best value of the video is only for the cases/flows that break or have gaps in them


Agreed. Once a flow passes, a video adds little; where it earns its cost is showing a failure so the fixer can see it. A few ways to make it pay off:

- One video per underlying cause, not per failing row. Several rows often break for the same reason. Record after we've grouped failures by cause, not during the first pass.
- Record each failure from a script that checks its own result. It shows the failure (red) now, and the fix PR re-runs the same script to show it passing (green). One piece of work gives you both the bug repro and the PR's demo.
- Gaps only get a video when someone has to decide. Examples: placeholder vs. warning for a missing source, or the periodic sync republishing imported pages. Gaps that already have a ticket just link to it.
- Passing rows get a checkbox and the build SHA, plus a screenshot where the result is visual.

From the code reading I'll mark the rows I expect to fail, so the bug bash tests those first and the videos go where the bugs are. Recording stays in a separate session, as you prefer.

**The ticket names the wrong attribute.** Asset re-upload is gated by `getSharedRoamNodesWithFullContentUpdatesSince`, which matches a node when either the page's own `:edit/time` or its `:page/edit-time` is newer than the watermark. `:page/edit-time` tracks the latest edit anywhere on the page, descendant blocks included. | -- | -- | -- | -- |
| rewrite a block with its own string | yes | no | **yes** |
| `props` on a block | yes | no | no |
| `props` on the page | yes | yes | no |
| create then delete a scratch child block | yes | no | no |
| rewrite the page with its own title | no | no | no |
| set `:page/edit-time` or `:edit/time` directly, four spellings | no | no | no |

Rewriting a block with its own string is the cheapest bump and it does move the time. It also reassigns `:edit/user`, and the replacement has no `:user/display-name`, so the sync would publish that node's `author_name` as "Anonymous User". That was confirmed against a real block, not a fixture. It is not an option.

That leaves two: create and delete a scratch child block, or a `props` write.

**The question.** Your wording may rule out `props` entirely. The intent read more as reducing complexity, and on that measure `props` is the simpler of the two options left.

A `props` write on the node's first child is one atomic write. It moves only `:page/edit-time`, so only the content path re-runs and the node row is left alone. It leaves `:edit/user` untouched, verified on September 18 against a block another user last edited. Writing the same constant value twice still moves the time, so the value is a constant, nothing ever reads it back, and there is no attempt count, no limit, and no per-node state.

Create-and-delete a scratch child block is the alternative. That is two writes with a state in between, and if the sync dies there it leaves an empty bullet behind on the user's page, which is the visible residue this approach is meant to avoid. More moving parts, not fewer.

Either one is fine to build. Pick one and the Solution and Notes get corrected to match.

Two cases deserve early attention: equal source-local IDs in different spaces, because Obsidian discovery currently filters on that ID alone; and relation changes after import, because refreshing node content may not reconcile the surrounding relations. name: scope-check
description: Compare a pull request or Git diff with a Linear engineering ticket's Done When criteria and produce a copy-ready PR scope check. Use when preparing or reviewing a PR, checking whether an implementation introduced broader abstractions or unsupported cases, or documenting why added scope is required now.
---

# Scope Check

Compare the completed change with its acceptance boundary. Return a copy-ready `Scope check` section unless the user requests the analysis too.

## Gather the Inputs

1. Resolve the Linear issue from an explicit `ENG-###` identifier, then from the PR or branch name. Fetch the issue with the Linear connector. If it is unavailable, ask for the ticket's `Problem`, `Solution`, and `Done When` sections.
2. Treat `Done When` as the acceptance boundary. Use `Problem` and `Solution` only to clarify that boundary, not to silently expand it.
3. Resolve the final change set from the supplied diff or PR. For a PR, inspect its metadata and complete diff. For the current branch, compare it with the PR base branch and include staged and unstaged changes.
4. Read linked decisions or ticket comments only when they explain an apparent scope expansion.

## Evaluate Scope

Map every material behavior or architectural change to a `Done When` criterion.

- Treat implementation details, tests, documentation, and generated files required to satisfy `Done When` as in scope.
- Flag broader abstractions, unrelated refactors, new dependencies, migrations, or support for cases not required by `Done When`.
- Do not treat a change as in scope only because it is useful or adjacent.

For each scope expansion, determine:

1. What broader abstraction or additional case was introduced?
2. Which current use case or ticket requires it, and why must it be included now rather than deferred?
3. Was anyone affected or consulted, and where is the discussion or decision recorded?

Do not invent missing justification. Mark it `Not documented` and recommend recording it in a Linear comment before the PR is merged.

## Format the Result

Use this form when the diff stays within scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: None.
```

Use this form when the diff expands scope:

```markdown
## Scope check

- [x] Ran `$scope-check` against ENG-#### and the final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`: <what changed>
- Required now: <use case or ticket and why it cannot be deferred>
- Anyone affected or consulted: <Yes, No, or Not documented>
- Decision: <link to the discussion or decision, or `Not documented`>
```

If the ticket or diff cannot be resolved, leave the checkbox unchecked and state exactly what input is missing. Keep findings short and evidence-based.

Do not modify the issue, PR, or implementation unless the user explicitly asks.
## Reviewer brief

<!-- Optional. Remove this section when it adds no value.
Include only the fields that help the reviewer:
- Result: The final behavior or outcome.
- Review focus: A decision, risk, or part of the diff that needs careful review.
- Risk or follow-up: Unresolved, unverified, or deferred work that affects approval.
-->

## Verification

<!-- Optional checks and their results. Remove this section when it adds no value. -->

## Loom video

<!-- Include a short Loom video for every PR (any change—UI, backend, refactors, infra, etc.).
This helps reviewers understand intent quickly and catches issues earlier
- Keep it under 2–3 minutes
- Show before/after for bug fixes
- Narrate key design or dev decisions
- Paste the Loom link in the PR body
-->

## Scope check

- [ ] Ran `$scope-check` against the ENG ticket and final diff.
- Scope beyond `Done When`:

<!-- Add either:
- `None` when the final diff stays within Done When.
- What changed, why it is required now, whether anyone was affected or consulted, and links to the use case, ticket, or decision.
-->

## Standards check

- [ ] Ran `$dg-pr-adherence-check` against the final diff and PR metadata.

<!-- Checking the box means the review ran, not that every requirement passed.
Make any outstanding findings or unverified requirements known to the PR author
so they can address them. -->

## Local delegated full review

- [ ] Ran a comprehensive review of the entire final diff in a subagent with a fresh context. Use `$dg-delegated-full-review` when no other full-review workflow is available.
"}}

+**Combined Roam–Obsidian validation**
+
+This run is prepared to find gaps between features when they are used together. Start from the combined local build described in [BASELINE.md](BASELINE.md). The full [test matrix](TEST-MATRIX.md) contains 100 scenarios and [results.json](results.json) expands them into 346 direction-specific executions. All manual executions start as **Not run**.
+
+**What the project promises**
+
+The [current Linear project](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/project/push-and-pull-nodes-between-roam-and-obsidian-49473d9eeb09) defines a group-targeted, single-node publish flow through shared persistence. Existing source sync keeps already-shared content fresh. Destination discovery, import, and refresh are explicit. A refresh may overwrite edits to the imported copy. Multiple selected imports are supported.
+
+Required dependencies include the node's schema, resolvable assets, Source where accessible, and eligible relations whose endpoints can resolve. This does not promise automatic remote polling, bidirectional content merge, full recursive graph export, automatic incompatible-schema merging, or exact preservation of every app-specific formatting feature.
+
+The source and destination are distinct spaces in every direction. RR does not mean two tabs of the same graph. Same-graph collaboration is an additional test dimension.
+
+| Route | Source | Destination |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| RR | Roam graph A | Roam graph B |
+| RO | Roam graph A | Obsidian vault B |
+| OR | Obsidian vault A | Roam graph B |
+| OO | Obsidian vault A | Obsidian vault B |
+
+Treat RO and OR as separate implementations. A successful round trip through converters is also different from a user completing publish, discovery, import, and refresh in the products.
+
+**People, spaces, and access**
+
+Use dedicated fixtures with known authors and a unique prefix such as `BB-20260925-<tester>-<case>`.
+
+| Actor | Role | Membership |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| A | Source author and fixture-group admin | G-team and G-other |
+| B | Collaborator/importer | G-team only |
+| C | Third collaborator | G-team and G-other |
+| X | Negative-access test account | Neither group |
+
+For the full matrix, provision distinct Roam graphs R-A, R-B, R-C and Obsidian vaults O-A, O-B, O-C. Reuse them across cases with unique fixture IDs. A and B also need separate authenticated sessions in the same Roam source graph for C05/C06, and in the same Roam destination graph for C07. Product graph access and DG group membership must be recorded separately; sharing a Roam graph does not test isolation between DG groups.
+
+A minimal first pass needs two Roam graphs, two Obsidian vaults, and a third destination added for C01. For complete three-space coverage, use all eight platform assignments: RRR, RRO, ROR, ROO, ORR, ORO, OOR, OOO. The three letters are A's, B's, and C's products; their spaces remain distinct.
+
+Use an isolated scratch vault for copied-vault identity tests. Multi-client Obsidian file synchronization is an additional host-product setup, not a DG promise.
+
+**Reusable fixture set**
+
+1. Source S with a citation, body text, and a known author.
+2. Evidence E referencing S; Evidence E2 also referencing S; a variant with no accessible Source.
+3. Claim C and Question Q; stored directed relations linking C, E, and Q.
+4. A custom node type with a format, Source role, and template body; one matching local type and one deliberately incompatible same-name type.
+5. Text payload with numbered version markers, nested blocks/lists, headings, paragraphs, code, links, tasks, and Unicode.
+6. Small valid PNG, PDF, audio, and video files. Reuse one file across nodes, and create different bytes with the same filename. Add valid boundary-size files around 6 MiB.
+7. Collision fixtures: equal titles, titles that normalize identically, equal source-local IDs in distinct spaces, and an unrelated existing local node at the intended destination title/path.
+8. A source node shared only to G-other and a public-to-G-team Evidence/relation that refers to it. This exercises dependency visibility without needing real private material.
+
+Record origin RIDs, local UIDs/paths, authors, groups, source timestamps, and content markers before each mutation. Shared storage inspection should use the same account permissions as the user action; an admin/service-role query cannot prove the recipient has correct access.
+
+**First-session order**
+
+Run workflows that reuse the same fixtures. The complete matrix is a coverage inventory, not a requirement to execute 346 separate setup procedures in one meeting.
+
+| Wave | Exercise | Cases covered | Route coverage |
+| --- | --- | --- | --- |
+| 1 | Publish a fresh text node, discover/import, repeat, edit upstream, manually refresh, rename | S01, I01, I08, U01, U02, U05 | All four directions |
+| 2 | Import Evidence alone with available, existing, and private/missing Source; repair a placeholder | D01–D04, S08 | All four directions; placeholder repair on RR/OR |
+| 3 | Add media after first share, refresh, reuse the asset, fail and retry one transfer | A01, A03, A07–A10, U10 | All four directions for media; route-specific retry paths |
+| 4 | Import a new relation schema and instance, accept separately, use on canvas | T02, T07–T12, T16 | All four directions, with both products' acceptance UIs |
+| 5 | A owns a; B imports a, relates owned b to a, publishes b; A and C import b | C01, C02, C11 | Start ROR and ORO; then homogeneous controls and remaining combinations |
+| 6 | Revoke access, test outsider reads, and recover after regrant | S04–S08, F01, F04 | Both destination products and both origin products |
+| 7 | Two users in one Roam graph: edit, asset retry, overlapping sync/import, provenance | C05–C08, A11 | Roam source to R/O; R/O source to shared Roam destination |
+| 8 | Target the known seams: IDs, normalized filenames, changed schema/Source, relation deletion | I07, I09, U11, T03, T14 | Each applicable path; resolve characterization questions |
+
+Check S10 before a Roam import session. With the current known command-gating gap, suggestive mode may need to be enabled to continue other cases. Record that prerequisite and leave S10 marked as the known gap; do not treat the workaround as a pass.
+
+Then use F05–F14 for the combined UX/recovery sweep and the remaining P1 cases for boundary coverage. Prioritize a distinct source/destination path over repeating an already covered actor/setup combination. Expand any failure across the other directions to establish its extent.
+
+**How to record a result**
+
+Record one result per case and route. Include candidate commit/build hashes, app versions, users and memberships, source/destination identifiers, fixture RIDs, before state, exact action, expected and actual behavior, and screenshot/log/storage evidence. A pass needs the visible result and stable identity/content; it cannot be inferred from a success toast alone.
+
+Use `Pass`, `Fail`, `Blocked`, `Decision needed`, or `Not run`. Record a known-gap failure against its existing issue. A blocked prerequisite is not a failed downstream feature. A characterization question needs a decision before an ambiguous outcome can be called a pass. Keep deferred polish separate from data loss, access leakage, wrong identity, unrecoverable partial imports, or broken core flows.
+
+A minimal useful bug report is: case + route + build; actors/groups; starting data; reproduction steps; expected versus actual; affected identity/content; evidence; workaround; existing related issue. Do not create duplicate tickets for behavior already covered by ENG-2297, ENG-2295, or the recorded asset retry limitations.
+
+After each destructive fixture operation, verify that only the named fixture changed. Preserve enough failed state to reproduce the problem, and record fixture cleanup separately from product behavior.
+
+**Proposed internal-release gate**
+
+Require core publish/import/refresh, Source, relation acceptance, media, access, and identity workflows in every applicable direction, plus the three-space and shared-Roam-user checks. Every open P0 failure needs a fix or an explicit team decision before calling the candidate ready. Product-policy questions and accepted limitations must be recorded rather than converted into assumed passes. This proposal does not mark the Linear validation task complete.
+
+Local type checks, unit tests, and compilation are prerequisites. This preparation does not yet prove runtime behavior, live RLS/storage access, schema deployment, or multi-user synchronization on the shared backend.

I’ve assembled the combined candidate and written **100 test scenarios**, with steps, expected results, applicable directions, and links to the existing work.

The main artifacts are:

- **[Full test matrix](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925/validation/roam-obsidian-2026-09-25/TEST-MATRIX.md)** — all 100 scenarios.
- **[Setup and session order](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925/validation/roam-obsidian-2026-09-25/README.md)** — people, groups, fixtures, and a practical sequence.
- **[Baseline and known gaps](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925/validation/roam-obsidian-2026-09-25/BASELINE.md)** — exact PR heads, integration decisions, and unresolved expectations.

**The combined build is ready for internal testing. Manual product validation has not been run yet.**

The candidate is at commit `09d97321` on `validation/roam-obsidian-20260925`, in [this dedicated worktree](/mnt/data/projects/dg-sync-validation-20260925).

It combines current main with:

| PR | Included work |
|---|---|
| [#1383](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1383) | Review and accept imported relation types and triples |
| [#1475](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1475) | Consistent schema metadata between sync and publish |
| [#1477](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1477) | Retry failed Roam asset copies |
| [#1479](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1479) | Roam import dialog and feedback |
| [#1482](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1482) | Obsidian import filenames |
| [#1412](https://github.com/DiscourseGraphs/discourse-graph/pull/1412) | Round-trip tests, adapted to current main |

The five runtime merges were clean. The older round-trip test stack needed small harness updates and the current `[[@placeholder]]` expectation. The explicitly iceboxed post-v0 refactors are excluded; the baseline records the other exclusions.

Loadable, production-configured bundles are available here:

- **[Roam extension folder](/home/sid/Downloads/roam-obsidian-bugbash-20260925-09d97321/roam)**
- **[Obsidian plugin folder](/home/sid/Downloads/roam-obsidian-bugbash-20260925-09d97321/obsidian)**

Frozen install, all eight workspace type-check tasks, all six unit-test tasks, and both builds pass. That includes **600 Roam tests and 87 Obsidian tests**. The exported bundles are hash-verified.

The testing model needs **four directed paths: RR, RO, OR, OO**. RO and OR exercise different implementations. Alongside those, we need multiple users in one Roam graph and three distinct collaborating spaces.

One expectation from Linear matters throughout: **source edits sync to shared storage; destination refresh is manual, and refresh may overwrite edits to the imported copy**. Automatic destination updates and bidirectional text merging are outside v0. This resolves the uncertainty about polling in the older sheet. [Project scope](https://linear.app/discourse-graphs/project/push-and-pull-nodes-between-roam-and-obsidian-49473d9eeb09)

The inventory covers:

| Area | Cases | What we exercise |
|---|---:|---|
| Sharing and access | 12 | First publish, multiple groups, outsiders, revoked/restored access, private dependencies, login changes, sharing/suggestive-mode combinations |
| Import, content, and identity | 12 | Markdown structure, filenames, duplicate titles, repeated imports, mixed batches, equal local IDs from different spaces |
| Updates and refresh | 12 | Source edits, local edits, rename, refresh-all partial failures, deletion/recreation, asset changes, Source/schema-only changes |
| Assets | 12 | Images/PDF/audio/video, paths, deduplication, same filename with different bytes, replacement, size limits, failures and retries |
| Source documents | 10 | Automatic Source import, reuse, missing/private Sources, placeholder repair, multiple Sources, changed references, returning to an original Source |
| Schemas and relations | 16 | Existing/new types, metadata consistency, templates, provisional schemas, instance acceptance, missing endpoints, deletion, direction, canvas use |
| Collaboration | 12 | Three-space relations, private endpoints, cycles, fan-out, multiple Roam editors, overlapping sync/import, authorship, cloned identities |
| Recovery and combined UX | 14 | Partial batches, relations failing after nodes succeed, interruption/restart, sorting/selection, result links, provenance, returning to normal work |

Expanding every applicable direction gives **346 individual executions**. That is the coverage inventory; the session guide groups them into workflows that reuse fixtures.

The most valuable combined-work scenario is this:

1. **A publishes node `a`.**
2. **B imports `a`, creates its own node `b`, relates `b` to imported `a`, and publishes `b`.**
3. **A imports `b` and should connect it to its original `a`.**
4. **C imports both and should see the correct tentative relation between those origins.**

Then repeat with C lacking access to `a`, with renamed endpoints, and after acceptance and refresh. This simultaneously exercises origin identity, group access, endpoint mapping, schema acceptance, and deduplication. The matrix includes all eight three-space platform combinations.

A second essential workflow uses **two people in the same Roam source graph**: A publishes, B edits the body or adds an asset, and either client performs the sync. We need to verify freshness, retry behavior, and authorship together.

There are already several specific places to probe:

- **ENG-2297 remains unresolved.** The candidate still gates Roam import discovery on suggestive mode. This is a known gap to record separately from subsequent import tests.
- **Obsidian discovery may conflate equal local IDs from different spaces.** Discovery filters on the local ID alone, while materialization uses fuller identity. This is a source-based risk, not a live reproduction.
- **Node refresh does not establish relation reconciliation.** Upstream relation deletion, retargeting, and preservation of local acceptance need explicit testing and a clear expected policy.
- **Asset recovery differs by failure location.** Sync failures can retry automatically; publish failures require republishing; assets reached only through another page’s embed have an accepted retry limitation.
- **Source-only and schema-only changes need their own cases.** Timestamp-based skipping can make these behave differently from editing the Evidence body.

I’d start with the four basic publish/import/refresh paths, then Source and media regressions, relation acceptance, the three-space workflow, and the shared-Roam-user/access cases. Those combinations should expose the most consequential gaps between the separately completed features.

 A good idea can be if we make a pr for it and then for a bunch of grouped tests you make one testing video and we attach to the pr wdyt??? what are other better ways to do this??

**Yes, a draft validation PR with one video per group of tests is a good fit here.** It gives us a concrete combined build, CI results, and one place for the team to inspect the work.

I’d add a small test-results table alongside the videos. The videos show what happened; the table makes coverage, failures, and remaining work easy to see.

The setup I’d use is:

1. **One draft integration PR for the combined candidate.** Its description names the included PRs and links to the test plan and loadable builds. We explicitly mark it as a validation branch, since its diff contains work already being reviewed in other PRs.
2. **Group tests around complete user workflows.** For example, publish → import → edit → refresh; Evidence with Sources and assets; or three-space collaboration with relations. Each recording follows a coherent workflow and identifies the cases it covers.
3. **One result entry per group and candidate version.** Record the commit, directions tested, pass/fail/blocked cases, video, and linked bugs.
4. **Fixes go into focused PRs.** We incorporate them into the combined candidate, rerun the affected group, and run a small cross-product smoke check.

The important detail is **pinning each recording to the build it tested**. Once we add another fix, an earlier video remains evidence for the earlier candidate. We should be able to tell which results still apply and which need a rerun.

For recording logistics, I’d capture the testing session as we execute it, then attach a short walkthrough of each completed group with timestamps or case IDs. That preserves useful failure evidence while giving reviewers something manageable to watch. A group with failures still gets a recording and an honest result.

There are three reasonable places to organize this:

| Approach | Strength | Tradeoff |
|---|---|---|
| **Draft PR as the main home** | Code, build, CI, discussion, and videos are together | The combined diff can be noisy; the PR changes as its constituent PRs merge |
| **Linear validation ticket as the main home** | Stable place for progress, blockers, bugs, and the release decision | Needs links back to the exact candidate build |
| **Shared test sheet as the main home** | Easiest for several developers to record results simultaneously | Needs disciplined links to commits, evidence, and issues |

**My preference is a light hybrid: the draft PR holds the candidate and videos; the existing internal-validation ticket holds the overall outcome and blocking bugs.** We keep one authoritative results table and link to it from both.

For our first few videos, I’d group them like this:

- **Basic lifecycle:** all four directions, repeated import, upstream edits, refresh, and rename.
- **Sources and assets:** available/missing Source, placeholder repair, media, deduplication, and retry.
- **Relations and collaboration:** schema acceptance, instance acceptance, canvas use, and A → B → C.
- **Access and recovery:** private dependencies, revoked access, partial failure, and multiple users in one Roam graph.

That gives us a reviewable record of the combined product, with a clear route from a failed test to its fix and retest.

Agreed. Once a flow passes, a video adds little; where it earns its cost is showing a failure so the fixer can see it. A few ways to make it pay off:

- One video per underlying cause, not per failing row. Several rows often break for the same reason. Record after we've grouped failures by cause, not during the first pass.
- Record each failure from a script that checks its own result. It shows the failure (red) now, and the fix PR re-runs the same script to show it passing (green). One piece of work gives you both the bug repro and the PR's demo.
- Gaps only get a video when someone has to decide. Examples: placeholder vs. warning for a missing source, or the periodic sync republishing imported pages. Gaps that already have a ticket just link to it.
- Passing rows get a checkbox and the build SHA, plus a screenshot where the result is visual.

From the code reading I'll mark the rows I expect to fail, so the bug bash tests those first and the videos go where the bugs are. Recording stays in a separate session, as you prefer.
